talk.title: People I like
talk.task: Tell Claude: “I like to spend time with people who…” and “I don't like people who…”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time: What kind of friends do you like to spend time with? What kind of classmates or co-workers do you not like to spend time with? What kind of teacher is the best? I answer with an adjective clause: I like to spend time with friends who tell a lot of jokes. Check: who/that for people, the verb agrees with the noun (people who talk, a friend who talks), no extra he/she/they.

talk.title: What kind of…?
talk.task: Claude asks: What kind of cities do you like to visit? What time of day do you feel most energetic?
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time: What kind of people do you like to spend time with? What kind of people do you prefer to avoid? What kind of cities do you like to visit? What kind of teachers do you learn best from? What kind of place would you like to live in? What time of day do you feel most energetic? Encourage me to answer with adjective clauses (I like cities that ..., a place where ..., the time when ...). Check who/that/which/where/when and that I don't add an extra pronoun.

lesson.title: Learn: which one? or extra information?

items.title: Two kinds of clauses
lines: Tells us WHICH one → no commas.
Just extra information → commas.

items.title: A name? Use commas
lines: We already know who or what it is.
chips: The professor who teaches Chemistry 101 is an excellent lecturer.
Professor Wilson, who teaches Chemistry 101, is an excellent lecturer.
Hawaii, which consists of eight principal islands, is a favorite vacation spot.

items.text: Mercury which is the nearest planet to the sun is also the smallest planet.

items.title: With commas: no that, no dropping
lines: Use who, whom, which, whose, where, when.

levels.title: Most of whom
levels.full: Using Expressions of Quantity in Adjective Clauses

lesson.title: Learn: some of which, most of whom

items.title: quantity + of + whom / which
lines: People → of whom. Things → of which. Always a comma.
chips: In my class there are 20 students, most of whom are from Asia.
He gave several reasons, only a few of which were valid.

items.text: The mall has 200 stores, many of ___ are having sales this weekend.

items.title: Not them, not who
lines: Only whom, which, whose in this pattern.
chips: ✅ two of whom are repeating the class
❌ two of them are repeating the class (in one sentence)
The teachers discussed Jim, one of whose problems was poor study habits.
items.tip: More common in writing than in speaking.

items.text: The couple has 13 children, only a few of whom live at home. How many live at home?
items.why: only a few of whom = a few of the children.

lines: …, some / many / most / none / two / both + of whom (people) / of which (things).
Use a comma. Don't use them or who.

levels.title: …, which surprised me

lines: which is already the subject.

lines: Only when who / that / which is the SUBJECT.

items.title: Way 1: cut who + be
lines: Take out the pronoun and be.

items.title: Way 2: no be? Use -ing
lines: Take out the pronoun. Change the verb to -ing.
chips: an alphabet that consists of 26 letters → an alphabet consisting of 26 letters

items.text: English has an alphabet that consists of 26 letters. → an alphabet ___ of 26 letters
The girl (whom) I saw was Mai. Can you reduce it?

talk.title: What is it?
